steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on diffusion models for constrained domains: explain why existing Riemannian diffusion models don't cover manifolds defined by inequality constraints, why such domains matter, and summarize the two models we propose.

  - true for many processes, but not for most manifolds defined by inequality constraints
  - example: hypercube \left(-1,1\right)^{d} with Euclidean metric; Riemannian BM = Euclidean d-dim BM (\mathbf{B}_{t})_{t\in\left[0,T\right]} while \mathbf{B}_{t}\in\left(-1,1\right)
  - BM escapes w/ probability one -> Riemannian BM not defined for all times -> earlier frameworks do not apply
- Why constrained manifolds matter
  - wide variety of settings: polytopes, convex sets of Euclidean spaces
  - studied in many disciplines: computational statistics, robotics, quantum physics, computational biology
  - principled diffusion models directly on these manifolds = significant practical importance
  - data-scarce and safety-critical settings: constraints reduce degrees of freedom / prevent unwanted behaviour
- Existing sampling methods on constrained manifolds
  - sampling problems on such manifolds are important
  - flurry of Markov chain methods for sampling unnormalised densities
  - reflected Brownian motion; log-barrier methods; hit-and-run (polytopes)
  - this work: generative modelling counterparts through the lens of diffusion models
  - geodesic BM and reflected BM are continuous stochastic processes -> well suited to extend continuous Riemannian diffusion framework of the earlier works
- Our contributions
  - two principled diffusion models for constrained domains
  - (i) geodesic Brownian motion, using tools from log-barrier methods
  - (ii) reflected Brownian motion
  - extend time-reversal and score matching to both settings
  - experiments: convex polytopes, space of symmetric positive definite matrices; constrained conformational modelling of proteins and robotic arms
  - code available

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Diffusion models are a powerful new paradigm for generative modelling that was introduced recently. The way they work is this: noise is added to the data progressively, following a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE), which is called the forward noising process, until the data is approximately Gaussian. The generative model is then an approximation of the time-reversed process associated with it, which is called the backward denoising process. This backward process is also an SDE, and its drift depends on the gradient of the logarithmic densities of the forward process, which is referred to as the Stein score. The score is approximated using techniques from deep learning and score matching. Diffusion models have been successful in domains like images and text, and recently the framework was extended to a wide range of Riemannian manifolds. This makes them applicable to various important modelling domains from the natural and engineering sciences, including Lie groups like the group of rotations \mathrm{SO}(3), the group of rigid body motions \mathrm{SE}(3), and many others.

However, the Riemannian diffusion models introduced in the two recent works rely on a key assumption, which is that the stochastic processes they consider are defined for all times. This is true for a large class of stochastic processes, but it is not true for most manifolds that are defined via a set of inequality constraints. For example, take the hypercube \left(-1,1\right)^{d} with the Euclidean metric. There the Riemannian Brownian motion is the same as the Euclidean d -dimensional Brownian motion (\mathbf{B}_{t})_{t\in\left[0,T\right]} as long as \mathbf{B}_{t}\in\left(-1,1\right). But (\mathbf{B}_{t})_{t\geq 0} escapes from \left(-1,1\right) with probability one, so the Riemannian Brownian motion is not defined for all times, and the frameworks of those two works do not apply.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Diffusion models are a powerful new paradigm for generative modelling that was introduced recently. The way they work is this: noise is added to the data progressively, following a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE), which is called the forward noising process, until the data is approximately Gaussian. The generative model is then an approximation of the time-reversed process associated with it, which is called the backward denoising process. This backward process is also an SDE, and its drift depends on the gradient of the logarithmic densities of the forward process, which is referred to as the Stein score. The score is approximated using techniques from deep learning and score matching. Diffusion models have been successful in domains like images and text, and recently the framework was extended to a wide range of Riemannian manifolds. This makes them applicable to various important modelling domains from the natural and engineering sciences, including Lie groups like the group of rotations \mathrm{SO}(3), the group of rigid body motions \mathrm{SE}(3), and many others.

However, the Riemannian diffusion models introduced in the two recent works rely on a key assumption, which is that the stochastic processes they consider are defined for all times. This is true for a large class of stochastic processes, but it is not true for most manifolds that are defined via a set of inequality constraints. For example, take the hypercube \left(-1,1\right)^{d} with the Euclidean metric. There the Riemannian Brownian motion is the same as the Euclidean d -dimensional Brownian motion (\mathbf{B}_{t})_{t\in\left[0,T\right]} as long as \mathbf{B}_{t}\in\left(-1,1\right). But (\mathbf{B}_{t})_{t\geq 0} escapes from \left(-1,1\right) with probability one, so the Riemannian Brownian motion is not defined for all times, and the frameworks of those two works do not apply.

These constrained manifolds cover a wide variety of settings, including polytopes and convex sets of Euclidean spaces, and they are studied in a large number of disciplines, for example computational statistics, robotics, quantum physics and computational biology. So it is of significant practical importance to derive principled diffusion models that can operate directly on these manifolds. They would enable generative modelling in data-scarce and safety-critical settings, where constraints on the modelled domain may reduce the number of degrees of freedom or prevent unwanted behaviour.

Sampling problems on these manifolds are important, and a flurry of Markov chain based methods were developed to sample from unnormalised densities on them. Algorithms that are successful include the reflected Brownian motion, log-barrier methods and, in the case of polytopes, hit-and-run approaches. In this work we study the generative modelling counterparts of these algorithms, through the lens of diffusion models. Of the existing methods for statistical sampling on constrained manifolds, the geodesic Brownian motion and the reflected Brownian motion are continuous stochastic processes, so they are well suited to extend the continuous Riemannian diffusion framework that was developed in the earlier works.

In particular, we introduce two principled diffusion models for generative modelling on constrained domains. The first is based on the geodesic Brownian motion and uses tools from the log-barrier methods, and the second is based on the reflected Brownian motion. For both cases we show how the ideas of time-reversal and score matching can be extended to these settings. We show that these methods are useful in practice on a range of tasks on convex polytopes and on the space of symmetric positive definite matrices, which includes the constrained conformational modelling of proteins and robotic arms. The code for all our experiments is available here.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Diffusion models [1,2,3,4] have recently been introduced as a powerful new paradigm for generative modelling. They work as follows: noise is progressively added to data following a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE)—the forward noising process—until it is approximately Gaussian. The generative model is then given by an approximation of the associated time-reversed process, called the backward denoising process. This is also an SDE, whose drift depends on the gradient of the logarithmic densities of the forward process, which is referred to as the Stein score. This score is approximated using techniques from deep learning and score matching [5,6]. Building on the success of diffusion models in domains such as images and text, this framework has recently been extended to a wide range of Riemannian manifolds [7,8], broadening their applicability to various important modelling domains in the natural and engineering sciences—including Lie groups such as the group of rotations \mathrm{SO}(3), the group of rigid body motions \mathrm{SE}(3), and many others [9,10,11,12,13,14].

However, a key assumption of the Riemannian diffusion models introduced in [7] and [8] is that the stochastic processes they consider are defined for all times. While this holds for a large class of stochastic processes, it does not hold for most manifolds defined via a set of inequality constraints. For instance, for the hypercube \left(-1,1\right)^{d} equipped with the Euclidean metric, the Riemannian Brownian motion coincides with the Euclidean d -dimensional Brownian motion (\mathbf{B}_{t})_{t\in\left[0,T\right]} as long as \mathbf{B}_{t}\in\left(-1,1\right). With probability one, (\mathbf{B}_{t})_{t\geq 0} escapes from \left(-1,1\right), so the Riemannian Brownian motion is not defined for all times and the frameworks of [7] and [8] do not apply. Such constrained manifolds comprise a wide variety of settings—including polytopes and convex sets of Euclidean spaces—and are studied across many disciplines, from computational statistics [15], over robotics [16] and quantum physics [17], to computational biology [18]. Deriving principled diffusion models that can operate directly on these manifolds is therefore of significant practical importance, as they would enable generative modelling in data-scarce and safety-critical settings where constraints on the modelled domain may reduce the number of degrees of freedom or prevent unwanted behaviour.

As sampling problems on such manifolds are important [19,20], a flurry of Markov chain based methods have been developed to sample from unnormalised densities. Successful algorithms include the reflected Brownian motion [21,22,23], log-barrier methods [24,25,26,19,27,28] and, for polytopes, hit-and-run approaches [29,30]. In this work, we study the generative modelling counterparts of these algorithms through the lens of diffusion models. Among existing methods for statistical sampling on constrained manifolds, the geodesic Brownian motion [25] and the reflected Brownian motion [21] are continuous stochastic processes, and are thus well suited for extending the continuous Riemannian diffusion framework developed by [7] and [8]. In particular, we introduce two principled diffusion models for generative modelling on constrained domains, based on (i) the geodesic Brownian motion, using tools from the log-barrier methods, and (ii) the reflected Brownian motion. In both cases, we show how the ideas of time-reversal and score matching extend to these settings. We demonstrate the practical utility of these methods on a range of tasks on convex polytopes and on the space of symmetric positive definite matrices, including the constrained conformational modelling of proteins and robotic arms. The code for all our experiments is available here.
